title: Let AI Read First: Enhancing Reading Abilities for Individuals with Dyslexia through Artificial Intelligence
venue: CHI EA ’25 (Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that people with dyslexia often struggle with reading fluency, comprehension, and attention, while existing assistive reading tools can be costly, impractical in quiet settings, or may distort the meaning of the original text. The authors propose Let AI Read First (LARF), an AI-based reading presentation strategy that uses large language models to annotate text with HTML tags such as highlighting, bolding, and underlining so that important information is visually emphasized without changing the original content.

The study evaluated LARF in a between-subjects experiment with 150 adult participants recruited online through Prolific. Participants either had a medical diagnosis of dyslexia, were being assessed for dyslexia, or strongly suspected undiagnosed dyslexia. They were randomly assigned to read the same IELTS Academic passage in one of three conditions: unmodified text, a conventional Bionic Reading version, or LARF-generated GPT-4 annotations. Outcomes included reading time, recall questions, free-detail retrieval scored by GPT-4 and verified by humans, comprehension questions, and subjective usability/helpfulness ratings.

Results showed that LARF improved reading-related outcomes relative to the other conditions, especially retrieval performance, subjective satisfaction, and perceived helpfulness. Comprehension and recall trends also favored LARF, though some differences were not statistically significant. A post hoc analysis further suggested that LARF was particularly beneficial for participants with more severe dyslexia symptoms. The paper concludes that AI-generated annotations may be a promising accessibility technique for dyslexic readers and may extend to other reading scenarios, though the authors note several implementation and model-scale limitations.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family / ChatGPT product used here as a large language model to annotate text with HTML tags and to score participant responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the annotation model in LARF to mark important information in reading passages; also used with human verification to score participants' retrieval responses.

findings.finding_summary: In a between-subjects experiment with participants who self-reported dyslexia (final analyzed sample n=148; LARF n=48), GPT-4-annotated text via LARF improved reading-related outcomes relative to control and Bionic Reading. For recall, LARF scored 3.71 (SD=1.20) vs 3.44 (SD=1.74) control and 3.53 (SD=1.64) conventional; for retrieval, LARF scored 5.87 (SD=2.30) vs 5.51 (SD=2.38) control and 4.96 (SD=2.89) conventional, with the retrieval difference statistically significant (F(2,128)=3.465, p=.034).
findings.measure: Recall questions and retrieval detail score
findings.sample_size: n=148 (recall n=131? not_reported; retrieval n=131? not_reported; final analysis reported n=148 overall, with 138 for reading time and 138/129 for some analyses)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary between-subjects experiment with randomized conditions and quantitative outcomes, but it is not a full K-12 study and uses adult participants with dyslexia. The design is fairly strong, though some analyses are modest and not all outcomes are statistically significant.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are positive but generally modest in magnitude, and the paper does not report standardized effect sizes for the key literacy outcomes. The statistically significant retrieval improvement is meaningful, but overall the impact appears small-to-moderate rather than large.
